extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of 19th-century theatre history; readers interested in Edwin Forrest and theatrical criticism
extracted.subtask_description: A biographical / critical essay on the actor Edwin Forrest describing his career, public reception, conflicts with critics, and artistic qualities. Focus is on explaining causes of criticism and assessing his strengths and defects as an actor and public figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art versus nature (refinement of performance)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The perfected artistic actor does not bring before his audience the reality itself of life with all its interclinging entanglements of passion and muscle, but he drops the repulsive details, all unessential vulgarities, refines and combines the chief features, harmonizing and heightening them in the process, and shows the result as a free picture..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance in text: acting as art should be a refined, heightened reflection of nature rather than a literal reproduction; remove repulsive or unessential details, harmonize and heighten chief features so the stage-picture resembles the original without its ruggedness. Anti-pattern: presenting crude, unrefined 'reality' on stage without artistic selection or tempering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraint / economy of exertion (continence around strength)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The easy curbing of expenditure which is the divine girdle of art... The enchanting cestus of art is continence around strength.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: greatest artists temper their force with restraint; display of power must be accompanied by control and economy. Example/critique: Forrest sometimes lacked this final curbing of expenditure, which critics saw as a defect. Anti-pattern: unbridled excess of gesture and energy that lacks tempering and refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power and sincerity of performance
rubrics_metrics.description: “Exuberance of power and sincerity was the primary greatness of Forrest as a tragedian.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: forceful, sincere expression and emotional energy are core virtues in tragic acting. Note that the text treats this both as a principal merit and—if unchecked—as a potential limitation, so power should be employed judiciously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and distinctiveness of character
rubrics_metrics.description: “A man of fresh and decisive originality, who is and appears just what God and nature have made him... his frank and flexible spontaneity... implies a tacit contempt for their meek conformities and spirit of routine.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: individuality and frank spontaneity are artistic strengths even if they provoke conventional tastes; originality may disturb some audiences but is portrayed as a democratic ideal and a mark of authentic artistry. Anti-pattern: slavish conformity to prevailing manners and styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity to the character (doing justice to the rôle)
rubrics_metrics.description: “He strove to do the best justice in his power to the characters he impersonated, and would then leave the verdict to the instincts of the public and the unbiassed judgments of competent critics.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: an actor's responsibility is faithful, rigorous portrayal of the character; after honest effort, judgment belongs to the public and informed critics. Anti-pattern: pandering to critics or changing performance primarily to curry favor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence and impartiality of critics
rubrics_metrics.description: “The utter falsity, unfairness, shallowness, and absurdity which so often marked the dramatic critiques of the press, a large proportion of which were written by persons... ignorant of the elementary principles of criticism.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: valid criticism should be informed, principled, and impartial. The text warns against partisan, ignorant, or venal reviewers (e.g., those expecting tribute or flattery). Anti-patterns: prejudiced, unprincipled, or compensation-seeking critics who misrepresent performers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular/folk judgment as a corrective measure
rubrics_metrics.description: “The general average of theatre-goers were played upon in their manliest sympathies by him... the permanent judgment of the multitude is never grandly wrong, however pettily right the opinion of the opposing few may be.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: broad public appreciation is presented as an important and often reliable measure of an actor's worth, and can balance elite or partisan critical opinion. Use popular reception as a meaningful indicator of success and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of audience sensitivities and appropriate scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages noting that some play-goers—"faint ladies, spruce clerks, spindling fops"—found Forrest's robust portrayals shocking and complained of 'coarseness and ferocity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: recognize that different audience segments have varying tolerances; while not advising succumbing to timidity, the text acknowledges that extreme realism or violence may alienate sensitive viewers. Anti-pattern: toning down authentic force merely to pander to the most timid spectators (the author defends Forrest against such demand).

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional integrity and civic-minded patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of Forrest's conduct: refusing to propitiate critics for favor, supporting American dramatic literature, donating money for 'books purely American.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: virtues of honesty, independence from venal press practices, and active support for native literature are held up as professional and civic standards. Acts of patronage and encouragement of homegrown drama are positive professional measures.
